title: Specimen Identification and Two-Identifier Principles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply specimen identification by confirming patient identity with two patient-specific identifiers before any specimen is collected or labeled.
- Use two-identifier verification to match each specimen and its label to the correct patient and the corresponding laboratory order.
- Prevent mislabeled specimens by labeling at the point of collection, verifying at every handoff, and escalating any mismatch per policy.
- Apply standard precautions and bloodborne pathogen safety practices, including proper PPE, sharps handling, and spill response, when assisting with specimens.
- Recognize and report identification and labeling near-misses and errors to support laboratory quality and patient safety.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Matching a specimen to the right patient is like writing a student's name on a test paper before turning it in — without the name, the teacher can't give the right student the grade.

### Question 2

It is like a secret handshake with two steps: you need both the person's name and their birthday to be sure you have the right person.

### Question 3

Your name and birthday are special to you — like a key that fits only your lock — so they help the team be sure they have the right you.

### Question 4

A room number is like a parking spot — it tells you where the car is, not whose car it is.

### Question 5

You put the right name on the cup before you fill it, not after the drink is already made.

### Question 6

It is better to let the person say their own name and birthday, like spelling it out themselves, than to just ask them to agree with you.

### Question 7

Label the cup the moment you pour the drink, so no one forgets whose cup is whose.

### Question 8

A good label is like a nametag with the person's full name, birthday, and the time — everything needed to know whose and when.

### Question 9

If a library book is shelved under the wrong name, someone gets the wrong book — and in medicine, getting the wrong test result is far more serious.

### Question 10

If the name on the cup doesn't match the person, you don't scribble over it — you get a fresh, correctly labeled cup.

### Question 11

Treat every cup of liquid as if it might have germs, so you always put on your protective gloves first.

### Question 12

Washing your hands after taking off gloves is like washing your hands before dinner — it clears away anything you can't see.

### Question 13

You treat every umbrella as if it might be wet, even if you can't see rain — the same way you treat every sample as if it might carry germs.

### Question 14

Even if the barista knows your usual order, they still ask your name so they don't hand your drink to someone else.

### Question 15

If a friend can't tell you their name, you check the name written on their ID tag, not a guess.

### Question 16

A wristband is like a name tag at a big camp that stays on your wrist so counselors always know who you are.

### Question 17

Check the name on the homework against the name on the class list — they have to match.

### Question 18

Don't write names on all the cups before the party and then hand them out blindly — label each cup as you fill it for each person.

### Question 19

First check whose cup it is, then pour the drink, then write the name on it right away.

### Question 20

A paper with no name can't be graded — you get a fresh copy instead of guessing who wrote it.

### Question 21

The assistant is like the careful helper who double-checks the nametags and calls the teacher over if something seems wrong.

### Question 22

Getting the right name on the test is like putting the right address on a letter — the message only helps if it reaches the right person.

### Question 23

If two kids in class are both named Sam, the teacher uses their birthdays to tell them apart.

### Question 24

If you forget your birthday, the teacher looks it up on the class list rather than guessing.

### Question 25

Ask someone to tell you their own name and birthday, rather than just saying "you're Tim, right?" and getting a sleepy nod.

### Question 26

If the birthday on the class list is off by one number, the teacher double-checks the real records before calling roll.

### Question 27

When two classmates have almost the same name, the teacher always checks the last initial and birthday on every paper.

### Question 28

If the name on a homework paper is smudged, you ask the student to rewrite it cleanly instead of guessing.

### Question 29

Even if a friend packed your lunch, you still check that it's actually yours before you eat it.

### Question 30

If the time is missing on your homework, you put the real time you finished, not a made-up one.

### Question 31

If two lists show different names for the same desk, the teacher sorts it out before calling roll, not after.

### Question 32

If a friend won't say their name for a game, you gently explain why it's needed and get help from the teacher if they still won't.

### Question 33

For a little kid, you check the name on their wrist tag and ask the grown-up with them to confirm.

### Question 34

If someone can't say their own name, you check their ID tag and ask the person who came with them.

### Question 35

Writing the time on a science experiment tells everyone when it started, so the results make sense.

### Question 36

Signing your name on your artwork lets everyone know who made it, so they can ask you about it.

### Question 37

A barcode is like a scanner at the store that beeps to confirm the right item, but a person still double-checks.

### Question 38

A chain of custody is like a relay race log that writes down who held the baton at every step.

### Question 39

Carry the cup of juice in a sturdy bag with a lid, not loose in your pocket.

### Question 40

If a juice cup is leaking, you put on gloves and clean it up carefully with the grown-up's instructions, not with your bare hands.

### Question 41

Used needles go straight into the special hard box, the way you drop a used pencil into the bin without snapping it.

### Question 42

If you spill something yucky on your skin, you wash it off right away and tell the teacher.

### Question 43

When something spills, you put on gloves and clean it with the special spray, the way you clean up a mess properly at home.

### Question 44

You don't eat your snack in the room where messy science experiments happen, so germs don't get in your mouth.

### Question 45

When you pour juice for several friends, you label each cup as you fill it, not all at once from a pile.

### Question 46

Check the class list matches the student's name before you write it on their paper.

### Question 47

If a friend is wearing two name tags with different names, you ask the teacher to sort it out before the game.

### Question 48

When the teacher gives directions out loud, you repeat them back to be sure you heard right.

### Question 49

If two notes from the teacher disagree, you ask which one is right instead of doing both.

### Question 50

If you write the wrong name on a paper, you start a clean copy instead of scribbling over it.

### Question 51

A paper with no name and a paper with the wrong name are two different mistakes, but both need a do-over.

### Question 52

Getting the wrong test paper back is a big deal because the grade (or medicine) goes to the wrong person.

### Question 53

If you almost trip on a loose tile, you tell someone so they can fix it before someone falls.

### Question 54

If a name is spelled two different ways, the teacher checks the real record instead of guessing which spelling is right.

### Question 55

You put on an apron before a messy art project, deciding by how messy it might get, not by how busy you are.

### Question 56

When you might get splashed, you wear goggles and a mask like a scientist, not just gloves.

### Question 57

When your hands are covered in glue, you don't touch your face or the clean table until you wash them.

### Question 58

Helping a nervous friend by explaining each step in a kind voice makes them feel safer.

### Question 59

Before baking, you check you have the right recipe and all the right ingredients for this exact cake.

### Question 60

Even on the busiest day, the teacher still checks every name on the roll, not just some.

### Question 61

You talk to someone who can't hear well by facing them and using clear signs or writing, so they can answer correctly.

### Question 62

If someone speaks another language, you get a proper translator so everyone understands the name and birthday correctly.

### Question 63

For really important homework, you have a friend double-check your name is on the paper.

### Question 64

A log is like a class sign-out sheet that shows who went where and when.

### Question 65

If someone is asleep and can't say their name, you read the name on their wrist tag instead.

### Question 66

If the name on a friend's lunchbox doesn't match the class list, you don't deliver it — you ask the teacher first.

### Question 67

If you realize you grabbed the wrong cup after you've filled it, you stop and get a fresh, correctly labeled cup.

### Question 68

When two kids have almost the same name, the teacher uses extra stickers and double-checks so their papers never get mixed.

### Question 69

If a friend says one name but their name tag says another, you ask the teacher to check the records before doing anything.

### Question 70

First check whose cup it is, then pour, then write the name, then carry it carefully.

### Question 71

One clue (like a first name) isn't enough when lots of people share it — you need a second clue to be sure.

### Question 72

If someone almost slips on a wet floor, you fix the floor and add a sign, not just scold the person who walked there.

### Question 73

Even if everyone is in a hurry, you still buckle your seatbelt every single time.

### Question 74

You write down that you checked the name and birthday, so later everyone knows it was done.

### Question 75

If you spill white-out on the name, you start a clean paper instead of scratching at it.

### Question 76

If two kids' allergy lists got swapped, someone might be given a food they can't eat — that's why the name must be right.

### Question 77

Keep each friend's pencils in their own labeled pouch so nobody's supplies get mixed up.

### Question 78

If the scanner can't read a price tag, you print a new tag instead of scribbling over it.

### Question 79

You don't start an experiment without the teacher's written instructions first.

### Question 80

A yellow warning on the name list means 'double-check these two papers extra carefully.'

### Question 81

When you're not sure who is allowed to fix the sign-up sheet, you hand it to the teacher.

### Question 82

You walk back to get the real answer key instead of guessing from memory.

### Question 83

Once the cup leaves your hand, only the name written on it tells everyone whose it is.

### Question 84

If you might have grabbed the wrong paper from a messy pile, you stop and check before turning anything in.

### Question 85

If the names don't match and you can't fix it, you stop and get the teacher before going further.

### Question 86

Signing your artwork lets the teacher know who to ask if something is unclear.

### Question 87

When you don't know the class rule, you ask the teacher what the rule is instead of making one up.

### Question 88

If you have to redo a paper, you write the correct name on a fresh sheet, not fix up the old one.

### Question 89

It's like asking someone to write their own name on the paper rather than just nodding when you say it.

### Question 90

You've done it right when you check both the name and the birthday against the official list.
